channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of October 10-16, 1983 — Xerox Service Lifeline Reaches Osborne Owners
item.description: A fallen portable pioneer turns to an industry giant to keep its machines working. Osborne Computer Corporation, once the most visible name in portable computing, announced October 11 that Xerox would service Osborne products while the manufacturer operated under federal bankruptcy protection. The pact offers owners a measure of continuity after the company’s swift reversal left the future of its machines and support network uncertain. Also this week: Xerox Sunrise Claims a Ten-Hour Workday · FBI Raids Bring Modem Intrusion Home · Electronic Arts Puts Designers in the Spotlight.

item.title: Week of October 3-9, 1983 — Britain's BBC Micro Makes Its American Debut
item.description: Acorn aims its $995 package at U.S. classrooms, with teacher notes, networking ambitions, and a 50,000-machine production commitment. Acorn Computer brought one of Britain's best-known educational machines to the United States this week, formally unveiling an American BBC Micro package priced at $995. The October 7 debut placed the machine directly into the contest for school computer labs, where Apple and other established suppliers already had strong positions. Also this week: Issue 3 Spectrum Change Breaks Some Existing Programs · Sanyo's $2,100 Challenger Joins the IBM-Compatible Charge · Hewlett-Packard Puts 'Magic' at Your Fingertips.

item.title: Week of September 26-October 2, 1983 — Atari Dumps Truckloads of Games in New Mexico Landfill
item.description: Cartridges and equipment from the El Paso plant are crushed and buried as the console market’s inventory crisis becomes impossible to hide. Truckloads of Atari material rolled into the Alamogordo, New Mexico, municipal landfill this week, where workers crushed and buried cartridges and equipment shipped from the company’s El Paso plant. A September 28 New York Times brief fixed the disposal to this week, turning a grim inventory operation into the sharpest picture yet of the videogame business’s retreat. Also this week: GNU Call Asks Programmers to Build a Free Unix-Compatible System · Apple Cuts Lisa to $6,995 and Points Dealers Toward Macintosh · IBM’s Unannounced ‘Peanut’ Has the Home Market Guessing.

item.title: Week of September 19-25, 1983 — Apple Slashes Lisa by $3,000 as Sculley Resets the Company
item.description: A stripped-down $6,995 configuration aims to revive the pioneering graphical workstation while IBM seizes the middle of the personal-computer market. Apple Computer opened the week with a dramatic answer to sluggish Lisa sales: dealers were told that the $9,995 mouse-driven workstation would be offered in a stripped-down $6,995 configuration. The $3,000 cut followed new president John Sculley’s four-day tour addressing some 1,500 dealers in 25 cities, a public show of urgency from a company suddenly chasing IBM in the market it helped create. Also this week: FCC Clears Coleco’s Adam for the Holiday Computer Battle · Portable Computers Crowd the Road-Warrior Market · IBM’s Shadow Lengthens Across Personal Computing.

item.title: Week of September 12-18, 1983 — OSBORNE CRASHES INTO BANKRUPTCY
item.description: The portable pioneer seeks Chapter 11 protection after demand collapses and suppliers are left owed $45 million. SAN FRANCISCO — Osborne Computer sought bankruptcy protection September 13, a stunning reversal for the company that turned a suitcase-sized computer and a rich software bundle into one of personal computing’s first spectacular success stories. Also this week: Shakeout Reaches Computers and Cartridges · M.U.L.E. and Archon Turn Rivalry into Art · A Portable That Really Fits the Lap.

item.title: Week of September 5-11, 1983 — BIG BLUE SETS THE STANDARD
item.description: IBM compatibility redraws the personal-computer map as a booming market enters its first great shakeout. NEW YORK — The personal-computer business has reached the moment when a boom begins to choose its standard. TIME's September 5 survey reports that IBM, only two years after introducing its Personal Computer, has captured 26 percent of unit sales and displaced Apple from first place. Also this week: Games by Telephone Move Closer to Home · Draft-Aide Puts CAD on the Personal Computer · Young Computer Experts Teach the Teachers.

item.title: Week of August 29-September 4, 1983 — IBM's PC Standard Tightens Its Grip
item.description: The two-year-old IBM PC has taken the sales lead, inspired a compatible-machine industry, and left once-hot independents scrambling for position. NEW YORK — The personal-computer trade has rarely moved so quickly from open field to established order. TIME reports this week that IBM's Personal Computer, introduced only in August 1981, now accounts for 26 percent of unit sales and has displaced Apple from first place. Also this week: Ultima III Makes the Quest a Team Affair · Portable Computers Crowd the Departure Gate · Cellular Service Moves Toward the Marketplace.

item.title: Week of August 22-28, 1983 — A Desktop for Every Freshman
item.description: More than 800 new Clarkson students are to collect personal computers during orientation, turning a bold campus requirement into everyday academic equipment. POTSDAM, N.Y. — More than 800 Clarkson College freshmen arriving Thursday will receive an unusual addition to the standard orientation packet: their own personal desktop computers. United Press International reported the distribution on August 24, as the college prepared to put a machine directly into the hands of every member of the incoming class. Also this week: Christmas Computer War Crowds the Aisles · Dragon's Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon · Atari Clears the Deck for XL.

item.title: Week of August 15-21, 1983 — Apple Developers Confront the Lisa Software Puzzle
item.description: At Apple's August gathering, independent programmers see faster unreleased software—but face difficult choices about how to build for the graphical machine. Apple's Lisa has made the graphical office a commercial proposition, but the machine's future now rests with people deciding what to make for it. At a week-long Independent Developers' Conference at the Dunfey Hotel in San Mateo, programmers gathered to compare methods, inspect works in progress and learn how Apple's unfamiliar visual environment might become a software market. Also this week: Computer Games Grow Up: M.U.L.E. and Suspended Lead the Summer · A $16.95 3-D Space Game Lands on Timex/Sinclair · IBM's ‘Peanut’ Rumor Keeps the Market Guessing.

item.title: Week of August 8-14, 1983 — Apple Courts Independent Programmers on 'Lisa Day'
item.description: At a week-long developers' conference, Apple works to turn Lisa's mouse-and-window interface into a platform outside programmers can build on. Apple spent this week trying to convince independent programmers that its expensive graphical computer, the Lisa, deserves their labor. At a week-long Independent Developers' Conference at the Dunfey Hotel in San Mateo, the company opened Thursday, August 11, as 'Lisa Day,' walking outside developers through the machine's unusual mouse-and-window way of working and the tools available to write for it. Also this week: Atari Erases the 1200XL and Bets on Four New Computers · Coleco's Adam Forces the Home-Computer Market to Scramble · Laserdisc Cartoon and a Colony Auction Headline the Summer Games.

item.title: Week of August 1-7, 1983 — M.U.L.E. Turns the Atari Into a Four-Player Marketplace
item.description: Ozark Softscape and Electronic Arts mix land development, arcade action, and a live commodity auction into one unusually social computer game. A new game from designer Dani Bunten and Ozark Softscape asks Atari owners to gather around one machine and build an economy together. M.U.L.E., published by Electronic Arts, supports as many as four players, with the computer taking any empty places, and makes unusually direct use of the Atari computer family's four controller ports. Also this week: Seventeen New Computers Crowd the Fall Starting Line · Atari Sweeps Away Its Old Line for Four XL Computers · C and Scientific Software Reach the Personal-Computer Desk.

item.title: Week of July 25-31, 1983 — Commodore Slashes 64 Price to £229
item.description: A £116 British price cut puts a 64K color computer into the fiercest part of the home-micro market. Commodore has taken what Personal Computer News called a “scythe” to its British prices. Effective August 1, the recommended retail price of the Commodore 64 falls from £345 to £229, a £116 cut that moves the 64K color machine into direct contention with far less capable rivals. Also this week: Aquarius Finally Reaches Launch Day · Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home · KoalaPad Makes the Screen a Drawing Board.

item.title: Week of July 18-24, 1983 — Apple II Sales Reach One Million
item.description: Six years after its debut, the expandable 6502 machine crosses a landmark that shows how far personal computing has moved beyond the hobby bench. Apple Computer sold its one-millionth Apple II on July 18, giving the personal-computer business a round-number milestone few could have imagined when the original machine appeared in 1977. The figure belongs to the whole Apple II family, whose color graphics, expansion slots, and accessible design carried it from enthusiasts’ rooms into schools, offices, and neighborhood computer shops. Also this week: Commodore Threatens to Halve Software Prices · Whole Earth Maps a 40,000-Program Jungle · More Memory for Less in the Home-Computer War.

item.title: Week of July 11-17, 1983 — Nintendo Brings the Arcade Home With Its Family Computer
item.description: At ¥14,800, Nintendo’s red-and-white Famicom arrives with two controllers and three arcade conversions. Nintendo launched its Family Computer in Japan on July 15, placing a compact red-and-white cartridge machine on shop counters for ¥14,800. The name was quickly shortened to Famicom, and the proposition was direct: swap a cartridge and bring the speed and familiarity of the arcade into the living room. Also this week: Sega Enters the Living Room With the SG-1000 · Electronic Arts' M.U.L.E. Turns Economics Into a Multiplayer Contest · Infocom's Suspended Puts Six Robots Between the Player and Disaster.

item.title: Week of July 4-10, 1983 — Coleco’s Adam Promises a Complete Computer for Under $600
item.description: The summer CES sensation combines game compatibility, high-capacity tape, word processing and a daisy-wheel printer in one mass-market package. The most talked-about personal computer of the summer is not merely a keyboard in a box. Coleco’s Adam, the lead item in the July 3 Arcade Express after its Consumer Electronics Show debut, is being pitched as a complete household system: computer, keyboard, high-capacity tape storage, word processing, joysticks and a daisy-wheel printer for a promised price below $600. Also this week: The $600 System Becomes the New Battleground · Dragon’s Lair Turns the Arcade into a Cartoon Theater · Electronic Arts Gives Designers Star Billing.

item.title: Week of June 27-July 3, 1983 — Dragon’s Lair Brings the Cartoon Arcade
item.description: Cinematronics’ laserdisc cabinet turns Don Bluth animation into the year’s loudest coin-op, and the rest of the arcade is scrambling to keep up. Just weeks after the June Consumer Electronics Show handed the home-computer business its next big products, the arcade answered with a machine that played more like a movie than a game. Cinematronics’ Dragon’s Lair, in arcades from June 1983, drove a Pioneer laserdisc player with a joystick and a single sword button, jumping between pre-animated scenes of a knight named Dirk the Daring rescuing Princess Daphne from the dragon Singe. Also this week: Coleco Pitches Adam as the Family Computer · Atari Resets Its 8-Bit Line with the 600XL and 800XL · WarGames Makes the Modem a Summer Star · The Price War Bites the Family-Room Shelf.

item.title: Week of June 20-26, 1983 — Software's Hard Sell
item.description: A $1.5 billion industry learns packaging, promotion and hit-making. Personal-computer software is becoming a packaged-goods business. SRI International projects 1983 revenue of $1.5 billion, after $1 billion in 1982 and $600 million in 1981, and TIME counts at least 230 producers chasing annual growth near 50 percent. The machine may command the showroom, but the programs now determine what owners can actually accomplish. Also this week: Coleco's Adam Takes Aim at the Family Room · Atari Clears the Deck for Four XL Machines · Programs May Soon Travel by Telephone.

item.title: Week of June 13–19, 1983 — Software's Hard Sell Becomes a Billion-Dollar Business
item.description: Commodore readies roughly 70 titles, Lotus buys attention, and software makers learn the arts of packaging and promotion. Personal-computer software is becoming a mass-market business before shoppers’ eyes. SRI International estimates that Americans bought $1 billion worth of personal-computer programs in 1982 and forecasts $1.5 billion this year, growth fast enough to turn code once passed among hobbyists into a fiercely promoted consumer product. Also this week: Coleco's Adam Resets the Complete-Computer Price · Atari Sweeps the Deck for Four XL Machines · WarGames Turns Computer Anxiety into a Hit.

item.title: Week of June 6–12, 1983 — Coleco’s $600 Adam Steals the Summer CES
item.description: A complete computer, word processor, fast tape drive and letter-quality printer promises to turn a ColecoVision household into a home office. The busiest conversation at Chicago’s June 5–8 Consumer Electronics Show begins with an unlikely challenger. Coleco, best known for ColecoVision, has unveiled Adam: an under-$600 home-computer package built around a Z80 processor, a full-size 75-key keyboard, SmartWriter word processing, BASIC, a Digital Data Pack recorder and a daisy-wheel printer. Also this week: Atari Answers With XL Computers and a Writing System · Software Price War Breaks Out at CES · WarGames Makes the Home Modem a Movie Star.

item.title: Week of May 30–June 5, 1983 — Electronic Arts' First Five Games Reach Players
item.description: A young publisher treats programmers like recording artists—and ships a remarkably varied opening slate. SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO — Ten days before this week began, the small company called Electronic Arts made its first shipment. Its May 20 slate carried five titles—Archon: The Light and the Dark, Hard Hat Mack, M.U.L.E., Worms?, and Axis Assassin—out of a warehouse and toward computer stores. The boxes announced the company’s ambition before a disk was loaded: creators’ names appeared prominently, and the packages borrowed the scale and visual confidence of record albums. Also this week: WarGames Makes Home Computing a Summer-Movie Star · Portable and 16-Bit Machines Crowd the June BYTE · Modems Bring Computer Gamers Together.
